title: Weather & seasons
blurb: Talk about the weather and seasons using Czech's subject-less impersonal expressions — prší, sněží, je zima.

vocab.example: Jaké je dnes počasí? Podívej se z okna.
Prší, vezmi si deštník.
V horách už sněží.
Dnes je hrozná zima, obleč si bundu.
V červenci je tady vždycky horko.
Svítí slunce, pojďme na procházku.
Fouká silný vítr, vezmi si čepici.
Moje oblíbené roční období je podzim.

grammarNote.title: Impersonal weather expressions — no subject needed
grammarNote.text: Czech weather talk doesn't use a subject like English "it": there's no word for "it" in prší (it's raining) or sněží (it's snowing) — the verb alone, in the 3rd person singular, carries the whole meaning. The other pattern is je + adjective: je zima (it's cold), je horko (it's hot), je teplo (it's warm). Watch out for zima specifically — it's both this impersonal "cold" adjective-like word and the feminine noun for the season "winter" (jaro/spring is neuter, léto/summer is neuter, podzim/autumn is masculine, zima/winter is feminine). Context tells them apart: je zima describes the weather right now, while v zimě ("in winter") refers to the season — that v/na + case pattern for seasons (v zimě, v létě, na jaře, na podzim) uses the locative case, which is coming in a later lesson, so for now just memorize those four phrases as fixed expressions.

check.explanation: Prší means "it's raining" — an impersonal verb with no subject needed.
check.note: Sněží (snowing), fouká (windy), and prší (raining) are all the same impersonal pattern — learn them as a set.

check.prompt: „Je zima“ can mean either "it's cold" or refer to the season "winter", depending on context.
check.explanation: Zima does double duty: je zima (impersonal, "it's cold") versus v zimě ("in winter", the season). The surrounding words tell you which one is meant.
check.note: This overlap trips up learners who assume every Czech word has exactly one meaning.

check.explanation: Fouká vítr — literally "blows wind", another subject-less impersonal weather expression.
Negate impersonal weather verbs the same way as any other verb — just add ne- to the front: prší → neprší.

title: Hobbies & free time
blurb: Say what you like and don't like doing using mít rád + the accusative case, plus everyday hobby vocabulary.

vocab.word: Co rád/a děláš ve volném čase?
vocab.translation: What do you like to do in your free time?
vocab.example: Ahoj, co rád děláš ve volném čase?
Mám rád hudbu, hlavně rock.
Mám ráda kávu, ale ne moc silnou.
Ve volném čase rád čtu knihy.
O víkendu hraju fotbal s kamarády.
Každý den chodím na procházky se psem.
Nemám rád sport, radši čtu.
Jaký je tvůj koníček?

grammarNote.title: Mít rád + accusative — how to say what you like
grammarNote.text: To say you like something, Czech uses mít rád (literally "to have [something] dear") followed by the thing you like in the accusative case, not the nominative. Rád itself agrees with the speaker, not the object: rád if you're male, ráda if you're female, rádi if you're speaking for a group. That's separate from what happens to the noun after it — for feminine nouns ending in -a, the accusative swaps that -a for -u: hudba (music, nominative) becomes hudbu in Mám rád hudbu; káva (coffee) becomes kávu. Masculine inanimate and neuter nouns often look identical in nominative and accusative (fotbal stays fotbal), so the feminine -a → -u swap is the pattern most worth watching for. To say you dislike something, just negate the verb: nemám rád/ráda.

check.prompt: How would a female speaker say "I like music"?
check.explanation: Ráda agrees with a female speaker, and hudbu is the accusative form of hudba after mít rád.
check.note: Mixing up rád/ráda/rádi is a very common beginner slip — it marks the speaker's gender, not the object's.

check.prompt: In „Mám rád kávu,“ the change from káva to kávu happens because mít rád requires its object in the accusative case.
check.explanation: Correct — káva is the nominative dictionary form, but as the object of mít rád it must take the accusative ending, kávu.
check.note: This is the same accusative pattern from the a2-01 lesson, just applied to a new verb phrase.

check.prompt: Mám ___ fotbal. (I like soccer — male speaker)
check.explanation: A male speaker uses rád: Mám rád fotbal. (Fotbal stays the same in the accusative since it's masculine inanimate.)

check.prompt: Change this to how a female speaker would say it: „Mám rád knihu.“ → ___
check.explanation: Only rád changes to ráda for a female speaker — knihu (the accusative object) stays exactly the same.

title: Travel & transport
blurb: Buy tickets, ask about schedules, and use the prepositions of motion do/z/na to say where you're going and coming from.

vocab.example: Dobrý den, jednu jízdenku do Prahy, prosím.

vocab.translation: When does the next train leave?
vocab.example: Promiňte, kdy jede příští vlak do Brna?
Musím přestoupit, nebo jede vlak přímo?
Jedu na nádraží, odjíždí mi vlak.
Vystupte na další zastávce.
Odjezd autobusu je v devět hodin.
Příjezd vlaku je naplánovaný na dvanáct hodin.
Každé ráno jedu do školy autobusem.

grammarNote.title: Prepositions of motion: do, z/ze, and na + case
grammarNote.text: To say where you're going or coming from, the preposition decides the case. Do ("to", into an enclosed place, city, or country) takes the genitive: jedu do Prahy, jedu do školy (Praha → Prahy, škola → školy). Z/ze ("from", out of) also takes the genitive, and often uses the exact same noun form as do — only the preposition tells you the direction: jedu z Prahy ("I'm going from Prague"). Na ("to"/"onto") takes the accusative instead, and is used for a specific set of nouns treated as open or event-like spaces rather than enclosed buildings — nádraží (station), zastávka (stop), pošta (post office), and similar: jedu na nádraží, jdu na zastávku. There's no single rule for which nouns take na instead of do — it's largely a fixed list you learn noun by noun, the same way English speakers just learn "at the station" vs. "in the building" by habit.

check.prompt: Which phrase means "I'm going FROM Prague"?
check.explanation: Z Prahy uses z + genitive to express "from Prague" — the opposite direction of do Prahy.
check.note: Do and z often share the same genitive noun form (Prahy), so the preposition itself is what carries the direction.

check.prompt: Do and z both take the genitive case, just with opposite meanings ("to" vs. "from").
check.explanation: Correct — both prepositions govern the genitive; only their meaning differs.
check.note: This is a handy shortcut: if you know the genitive form of a place, you can use it with either preposition.

check.explanation: Do + genitive (školy) expresses motion into an enclosed place like a school building.

check.prompt: Turn this statement into a question asking when the NEXT train leaves: „Vlak jede v devět.“ → ___
check.explanation: Příští ("next") + jede ("leaves/goes") is the standard way to ask about the next departure at a station.
